extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for assessing inductive inference and for applying probability theory inversely to infer causes from observed events; includes limits of empirical verification, the necessity of deduction for certainty, and the inverse/probabilistic method (Laplace/Poisson style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite instances cannot prove a general law
rubrics_metrics.description: No finite number of instances can ever prove a general law, or can give us certain knowledge of even one other instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: numbers ending in 7 appear prime in a few trials (27, 57, 117 show counterexamples); the polynomial x^2 + x + 41 gives many primes for small x but fails at x=40; Babbage's machine could produce long sequences obeying a law and then break the law suddenly. Moral: empirical trials, however numerous, do not logically establish universal generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive demonstration required for certainty of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to have no confidence in any law until we have treated it deductively, and have shown that from the conditions supposed the results expected must ensue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation may suggest a law, but only deductive proof establishes generality. Historical examples: Newton's binomial theorem was suggested by observation but lacked demonstration until later mathematicians provided deductive proofs; Euclidean propositions required deduction beyond measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation suggests hypotheses but does not establish them
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery by observation 'means nothing more than suggestion'; only by pure deduction is the general law really established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galileo's observations of the cycloid suggested the area relation but could not prove it; measurement and trial can indicate patterns but cannot replace deductive proof. Use observation to generate hypotheses, then pursue deduction/verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification can only guard against accidental oversights, not replace deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical verification at most guards against accidental oversights; deductive reasoning yields absolute certainty when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In geometry, measurements are crude approximations; deductive proofs provide exact results or arbitrarily close approximations where appropriate (e.g., areas of sphere, parabola, cycloid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical truths require deductive proof rather than measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: No skill and care could ever enable us to verify absolutely any one geometrical proposition by measurement; deductive geometrical reasoning yields absolute certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: angles inscribed in semicircles being right angles cannot be established by measurement alone; purported angle-trisectors discovered by measurement were shown by deduction to be invalid or only special-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish certainty (of consciousness and logical inference) from probability (about natural facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever feeling is present to the mind is certainly known to that mind; fundamental laws of thought are certain; but inferences about natural objects are never certain except hypothetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: I certainly experience blueness; I can deduce logically that if A indistinguishable from B and B from C then A from C; but statements like 'gold is insoluble in nitric acid' are hypothetical and subject to misidentification or unrecognized differences among specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of misidentification makes inductive conclusions fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical confusions (e.g., strontia vs baryta, caesium and rubidium mistaken for potassium) show that confident inductive inferences may be falsified by mistaken identification of substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists must account for the possibility that observed specimens are not identical in unobserved respects; this undermines absolute certainty of many inductive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: No law of nature is absolutely safe from exception or reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Not one of the inductive truths which men have established, or think they have established, is really safe from exception or reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-established laws (e.g., universal gravitation) are conditional on extensive qualifications (all other circumstances being equal) and can be falsified by unexpected events (e.g., comet splitting or unknown perturbing bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume stationarity/stability between observation and inference
rubrics_metrics.description: In inductive inference we must assume that, between the time of an observation and that to which our inferences relate, no change in the 'contents of the ballot-box' (i.e., governing conditions) has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tacit assumption (no change in causal background) is necessary for projecting past observations to future cases; its violation is a source of inductive error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the inverse method (probabilities of causes proportional to likelihoods)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event can be produced by any one of a certain number of different causes, all equally probable a priori, the probabilities of the existence of these causes as inferred from the event are proportional to the probabilities of the event as derived from these causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally: posterior probability of cause Ci ∝ p_i, where p_i is probability of event given Ci; normalized by sum of all p_j. Illustrated by Laplace, Poisson's 'ballot-box' analogy, and explicit fractional formulae in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most probable cause is the cause that would most probably produce the observed event
rubrics_metrics.description: The most probable cause of an event which has happened is that which would most probably lead to the event, supposing the cause to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies intuitive causal reasoning and is formalized by the inverse method; demonstrations by Donkin, Boole, Poisson support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: When few hypotheses exist, calculate respective probabilities directly
rubrics_metrics.description: In many scientific inductions where only two or a few hypotheses can explain phenomena, one can often calculate their respective probabilities via the inverse method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bunsen and Kirchhoff used this to establish with near certainty that iron exists in the sun by computing the improbability of sixty spectral coincidences arising by chance versus the high likelihood if iron were present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combinatorics and permutation counts to assess improbability of chance patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the number of possible arrangements (e.g., 52! for a deck of cards) to show how extraordinarily unlikely certain ordered outcomes are by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a pack of cards in perfect numerical order is overwhelmingly unlikely by chance, leading us to infer intentional arrangement; permutation counts provide quantitative grounds for preferring causal hypotheses over chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact similarity between complex objects strongly indicates common origin
rubrics_metrics.description: When two objects (printed pages, engravings, coins, footprints) show near-perfect resemblance, the most probable explanation is common source (same type/plate/dies/boot) rather than independent creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical or human-made exact replication is far more probable than two independent agents producing identical complex details; this underlies methods in textual criticism and forensics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincident errors across documents provide strong evidence of derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The occurrence of the same peculiar mistakes (e.g., same misspelling) in multiple documents yields extremely small chance probabilities and supports derivation from a common source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative example: if each document has 10,000 words, probability of same random error is <1/10,000; multiple coincident errors multiply improbabilities and allow establishing genealogies of texts (e.g., logarithmic tables, New Testament manuscripts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical coincidences with vanishing chance probability can yield effectively certain inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: When the probability of casual coincidence is astronomically small, observing many coincidences justifies near-certain inference of a causal connection (e.g., iron lines matching solar spectrum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kirchhoff example: sixty coincidences of spectral lines has chance probability less than 1 in a trillion (or far smaller), so the hypothesis that iron exists in the sun becomes immensely more probable by the inverse method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability calculations are deductive in form even when applied inductively
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether probability is used deductively (predicting events from known conditions) or inductively (inferring conditions from events), the calculation follows deductive principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus inverse (inductive) probability arguments rest on deductive manipulation of likelihoods and normalization; understanding the rule of receding from event to causes is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of sensory measurement demand deductive/mental methods for high precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Senses and manual measurement soon stop while deductive reasoning can proceed to any required degree of approximation (e.g., calculation of π to many places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: attempts to measure π with compasses yield only a few correct digits; mathematical methods (Shanks' calculation to 707 places) are needed for arbitrary precision.
